Everything on these pages was written by RCF English. The rubrics are
classroom rubrics for feedback; they are NOT the official marking schemes
and must never be described as such. Official schemes are linked from the

and examinations are taken through an authorised centre (in Sri Lanka, the

pages.title: Assessment Rubrics for English
pages.metaTitle: Printable English Assessment Rubrics: Writing, Speaking, Reading Aloud, Literature
pages.description: Four printable classroom rubrics written by RCF English: guided and free writing, speaking, reading aloud, and literature answers, with four clear bands and advice on using them for feedback.
pages.keywords: English writing rubric, speaking rubric, reading aloud rubric, literature answer rubric, assessment rubric Sri Lanka, classroom assessment English

hero.text: A rubric tells a student what the next band looks like. That is its whole job, and it only does it if the words in each box are plain enough for the student to read.

blocks.title: Classroom rubrics, not examination marking schemes
text: These rubrics were **written by RCF English** for feedback and classroom assessment. You may print, copy and adapt them freely.

They are **not** the official marking schemes used for term tests or the G.C.E. examinations, and marks given with them do not predict an examination grade. For official schemes, see [Marking Schemes](past-papers/marking-schemes/).

blocks.heading: Using a rubric so that it teaches

items.title: Show it before the task, not after
text: Read the Band 3 column aloud with the class before they write or speak. A rubric first seen on the returned script is a verdict, not a guide.

items.title: Mark one or two rows, not all four
text: For a class set, choose the row the lesson was about. Marking every row on every script takes four times as long and gives the student four things to fix at once.

items.title: Circle the box, then write one line
text: Circle the band the work reached, and write one sentence saying what would move it to the next box. *To reach Band 3: give a reason for each point.*

items.title: Let students use it on each other
text: Pairs mark each other's work on one row only. They will be harsher than you, and they will learn the criteria faster than from any explanation.

blocks.heading: 1. Writing rubric (guided and free writing)
blocks.caption: RCF English writing rubric. Band 4 is the highest. Use for letters, descriptions, stories, reports and essays.
rows: Much of the task is missing or off the topic.
The main point is there, but one or more required parts are missing.
All parts are covered, with detail that suits the reader and purpose.
No clear order; ideas are hard to follow.
Some order, but paragraphs or linking are missing.
Clear beginning, middle and end, with paragraphs.
Well ordered throughout; linking words guide the reader smoothly.
Frequent errors make the meaning unclear.
Errors are common but the meaning is mostly clear.
Some errors, but they rarely affect meaning.
Few errors; a range of sentence types is used accurately.
Very limited; words are often wrong or repeated.
Precise, varied words chosen for effect.
Format ignored; punctuation and spelling weak.
Format partly correct; frequent punctuation or spelling errors.
Correct format; mostly accurate punctuation and spelling.
Correct format; punctuation and spelling almost always accurate.

blocks.heading: 2. Speaking rubric
blocks.caption: RCF English speaking rubric, for short talks, role plays, interviews and discussions.
rows: Says very little about the topic.
Makes one or two simple points.
Develops points with reasons or examples.
Frequent hesitation, but keeps going with help.
Speaks smoothly at a natural pace.
Some errors that do not block meaning.
Few errors, even in longer sentences.
Does not respond to the listener.
Listens, responds and keeps the conversation going.

blocks.heading: 3. Reading aloud rubric
blocks.caption: RCF English reading aloud rubric, for primary and lower secondary classes.
rows: Almost all words read correctly, including new ones.
Short groups of words, often broken.
Smooth phrases that follow the punctuation.
Voice changes for questions and speech.
Expression shows the meaning and mood.
Cannot say what the text was about.
Retells the main events or points.
Retells and explains why something happened.

blocks.heading: 4. Literature answer rubric
blocks.caption: RCF English classroom rubric for O/L and A/L Literature paragraph and essay answers.
rows: Touches on the question now and then.
Answers the exact question, including every part of it.
Short, well-chosen quotations placed exactly where needed.
No comment on language or technique.
Names a device but does not explain it.
Explains the effect on the reader and links it to the writer's purpose.
Clear paragraphs, each with one point.
A developed argument with a clear conclusion.

blocks.title: To print a rubric
text: Use your browser's print option and choose *Save as PDF* or print directly. Each table prints with its heading. To print only one, select it on screen and choose *Print selection* where your browser offers it.

pages.title: Term-Test Preparation Plans
pages.metaTitle: English Term-Test Preparation Plan: Six Weeks, Final Week and After the Test
pages.description: A practical six-week plan for preparing an English class for the term test, a lesson-by-lesson final week, and a simple way to analyse the results so the next term starts in the right place.
pages.keywords: term test preparation plan, English term test revision, first term test, second term test, third term test, revision plan Sri Lanka

hero.text: A term test is most useful as information for the teacher. The plan below prepares students properly and makes sure the results tell you something you can act on.

blocks.heading: Before you start
text: Find out three things first: **which lessons the test covers**, **how the paper is set out** (sections, marks and time), and **the test date**. In most schools the paper is set by the zone, the province or the school itself, so ask the person who sets it rather than guessing from last year.
Then look at a past term-test paper of the same kind with the class. The [Past Papers](past-papers/) section has term-test papers by grade, term and province.

blocks.heading: Six-week preparation plan
blocks.caption: RCF English six-week term-test plan. Weeks count backwards from the test.
rows: A short diagnostic: one question of each kind from a past paper, 20 minutes. Tally which kinds most students got wrong.
Students list the three topics they find hardest.
Re-teach the topic most students got wrong, with guided practice.
Ten short practice items on that topic.
Re-teach the second topic. One guided writing task using the task type in the paper.
Complete the writing task at home.
Timed reading passage with questions. Build a class word list from the unit texts.
Learn ten words from the list.
A complete past paper under test conditions. Mark it together the next lesson.
Correct their own mistakes in a different colour.
See the final-week plan below. No new content.

blocks.heading: The final week, lesson by lesson

items.q: Lesson 1: the paper, section by section
a: Walk through the paper layout on the board: each section, its marks and a suggested time. Students write the timing on the inside cover of their exercise book.
Point out where marks are most often lost: unanswered questions, ignored word limits, and questions that ask for two things.
Show five real mistakes from the practice paper, anonymously. Students correct them in pairs. Choose the mistakes that the most students made, not the funniest.
One writing task in exactly the time the paper allows. Stop them at the time, even if unfinished. The lesson is about finishing, not perfection.
A ten-question oral quiz on grammar and vocabulary, then students choose one topic they still fear and work on it with a partner who is confident in it.
Answer questions about the test. Remind them to read the whole paper first, answer the questions they know, and come back to the others. End early and on something they can do.

blocks.heading: After the test: a results tally
blocks.caption: Copy this into your record book. Count how many students lost most of the marks on each part of the paper.

blocks.title: Use the tally before you return the scripts
text: The part with the most students under half is where the first week of next term goes. Tell the class what you found and what you will do about it. Students take the next test more seriously when they see the last one changed the lessons.

hero.text: Choose a word set or type your own, pick a card style, and print. Every card set below was written by RCF English and is free to copy.

blocks.heading: Flashcard maker
intro: The word-and-meaning cards fold in half, with the meaning printed upside down on the lower half so it reads the right way once folded. Typed words stay on your own device.

sets.label: Classroom language

sets.label: Irregular verbs: base form and past
Linking words for writing

blocks.heading: Eight games that use the cards

a: Hold up a word card for one second, then hide it. The class says the word together. Speed up as they improve. Use large word-only cards.
Read a meaning aloud. The first team to hold up or say the matching word scores. With fold cards, the meaning side faces you and the word faces the class, so you never need a list.
Print a set twice, once word-only and once as fold cards cut into two halves. Cards face down; students turn two over and keep them if the word matches its meaning.
Stick eight cards on the board. Students close their eyes; remove one. The first to name the missing word comes out and removes the next one.
Give every student a card. Call a category: *stand up if your word is a feeling* or *stand up if your verb is irregular*. Those standing say their word.
Each pair draws three cards and writes one sentence using all three words. The best sentences are read aloud. Works well with linking words.
One student sits facing the class with their back to the board. A card is shown to the class, who explain the word without saying it. The student in the seat guesses.
For irregular verbs or linking words, give each student a card and have groups arrange themselves: base form next to past form, or first, then, finally in order.

hero.text: Professional development is not a certificate collected once. It is one deliberate change a term, tried in a real classroom and kept if it works.

blocks.heading: A plan for one school year

items.title: First term: choose one problem
text: Pick the single thing that costs your lessons most, such as students not speaking, weak paragraph writing, or losing the class in the last ten minutes. Write it at the front of your record book.

items.title: Try one change for six weeks
text: Read about the problem (see [Professional Reading](teacher-resources/professional-reading/)), choose one technique, and use it in every relevant lesson for six weeks. Note in one line after each lesson what happened.

items.title: Second term: be observed
text: Ask a colleague to watch twenty minutes of a lesson with only your chosen problem in mind. Use the [observation checklist](teacher-resources/lesson-plan-template/). Offer to do the same for them.

items.title: Share what worked
text: Tell your department, or the [teacher groups](about/online-communities/), what you tried and what happened, including what did not work. Explaining it is how it becomes part of your teaching.

items.title: Third term: look at the evidence
text: Compare student work from the start and the end of the year on your chosen problem. Keep the change if the work improved. Then choose next year's problem.

blocks.heading: The Cambridge Teaching Knowledge Test (TKT)
text: The TKT is a Cambridge English qualification that tests knowledge about teaching English. It is taken in **separate modules**, so a teacher can sit one module at a time. The three core modules are:
**Module 1: Language and background to language learning and teaching.** Grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation and the four skills described from a teacher's point of view, and how learners differ.
**Module 2: Lesson planning and use of resources for language teaching.** Planning lessons and choosing and adapting materials and activities.
**Module 3: Managing the teaching and learning process.** Classroom language, interaction, correction and managing learners.
The TKT tests knowledge rather than observed teaching, so it suits both practising teachers and people preparing to teach.

blocks.title: Who awards the TKT
bullets: The TKT is **awarded by Cambridge University Press & Assessment**. RCF English and RCF Online Academy do not award it and are not a test centre.
In Sri Lanka the examinations are taken **through the British Council**. Test formats, dates and fees are matters for the test centre, so confirm them with the centre directly.
